To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a rendering-aware, multi-track neural network can learn to extract and make sense out of multiple visual cues for SVBRDF estimation, (2) the network can be trained on synthetic data and generalize to real-world materials, (3) the network can recover normal maps and BRDF maps from a single image, and (4) the network can generalize to a variety of material classes.

(1) a rendering-aware network can be trained to recover spatially-varyng BRDFs from a single picture, (2) a large database of procedurally created SVBRDFs is needed to train a deep network to capture the wide diversity of materials in the real-world, (3) distant material regions provide complementary visual cues that are beneficial in the network training, (4) a network with both local and global feature propagation tracks is needed for accurate SVBRDF estimation, and

(1) we introduce an SVBRDF similarity measure that is differentiable with respect to the input maps and (2) we show that a network that combines convolutional and fully-connected tracks can be trained to recover spatially-varyng BRDFs from single images.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of recovering the appearance of an unknown object from a single picture.
the problem of single-shot appearance capture.
the problem of single-image material capture.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have developed a deep network for SVBRDF capture that works in single images.
our method is the first to demonstrate the possibility of capturing SVBRDFs from single images.
our method can recover SVBRDFs from single images with the same accuracy and robustness of the best methods in the literature, but with much less data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have trained a deep neural network that is capable of extracting and making sense of visual cues for material appearance from single images.
we present a deep neural network for SVBRDF capture that is trained on a wide range of materials and is able to extract the material properties from a single picture.
we present a deep learning-based approach to capture material appearance from a single image.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, with the right training data and network design, it is possible to learn a deep network that automatically extracts and makes sense of the visual cues that allow us to infer material appearance from a single image.
deep learning can be used to extract and make sense out of visual cues that are known to be important for material perception.
a rendering-aware deep learning network can be trained to automatically extract and combine visual cues to recover spatially-varyingly material appearance.
